newsitem.title: USA: Clinton stumps Western states in homestretch.
newsitem.headline: Clinton stumps Western states in homestretch.

text.p: President Bill Clinton glided into the homestretch of his re-election campaign on Thursday with sunny rhetoric about the country's prospects, barbs about his opponents' tactics and a touch of nostalgia.

Speaking to a large, cheering crowd in this desert playground, Clinton said: "Five days before this election, I want you to be upbeat about America, optimistic about your future and determined to make the choice that will guarantee that that vision can be made real."
"That is the choice" on Nov. 5, he said.
Clinton said there was "a real difference" between Republican Bob Dole and him on key issues "and I believe it's an honest difference."

"I don't like all this harsh rhetoric and personal attacks and attempts to convince people that your opponent is no good. I don't think there's very much to that," Clinton said in an indirect but unmistakable reference to Dole's relentless attacks on his ethics and character.

"I'm about to end my last campaign. I can tell you this," Clinton continued. "I've been working at this for over 20 years now. Most people I've met from both parties, from all points on the political spectrum, have loved our country, have wanted what was best for it, worked hard and were honest -- contrary to the image that is often portrayed."

Clinton's defence of career politicians came as new questions arose about a senior Democratic fundraiser's ties to the White House, fuelling a controversy that has dominated the final days of the presidential race.

The Washington Post and New York Times reported on Thursday that John Huang, who was suspended from his Democratic Party fundraising duties two weeks ago amid reports that he unlawfully solicited foreign contributions, had made at least 78 visits to the White House since July 1, 1995.
Citing records kept by the Secret Service, the Post said the number of visits suggested Huang had a closer connection to the White House than was previously known.
White House press secretary Mike McCurry said the frequency of Huang's visits was not unusual because he could have been "seeing a friend, going to a meeting (or) attending a large reception."
McCurry also insisted they were "consistent with his responsibilities" as a Commerce Department official and later as a party fundraiser.

A senior administration official accompanying Clinton said the reports were "making a mountain out of a molehill" and that Huang was "involved in fundraising and did outreach to the Asian-American community, which is of growing importance" as a voting block.
Clinton was to tackle the issue of campaign finance reform in a major speech in Santa Barbara, California on Friday.
Earlier on Thursday Clinton sought votes in Arizona, which no Democratic presidential candidate has won since 1948.

"Compared to four years ago, we have 10 and a half million more jobs, wer have the lowest combined rates of unemployment, inflation and home mortgage interest in 27 years," he said. "The deficit has been cut in all four years of my administration for the first time in the 20th century."

Asked if Clinton's effort to carry marginal states meant he was sure that he had the 270 electoral votes needed to win locked up, deputy campaign director Fred DuVal said: "We're not neglecting our base; we've simply expanded it."
All major polls are giving Clinton a lead nationally of between 10 and 18 points, except for the Reuters/Zogby poll which has Dole narrowing the gap to 7.7 points in recent days.

At the start of his speech here, Clinton turned a little nostalgic, recalling that his late mother, Virginia Kelley, "loved this community so much and loved to come here. I wish she were here with me still for this election," he said.
She died in January, 1994, days after visiting Las Vegas.
